original_excerpt: Malundi or owner of the mal is a shepherd who tends his own flock. But if someone is hired to look after the flock on wages, he is called a pohal... The pohals, when hired, are given (1) free meals, (2) free clothing and wool for the family, (3) two or four sheep per hundred sheep and goats and (4) Rs. 2/- in cash per month as wages.
neutral_summary: Differentiates owner-shepherds (malundi) from hired wage-shepherds (pohal), detailing customary remuneration in kind (food, clothing, wool, sheep dividend) and cash.
term_notes: Pohal derived from Pashupal; mal refers to pastoral flock.
coder_notes: Primary evidence of contractual pastoral labour in high-altitude transhumance.

original_excerpt: No one keeps a buffalo as the climate is not conducive to the proper rearing of buffalo. Once a villager brought a buffalo, but he was not happy with the experience as the milk yield suddenly dropped from 9 srs. to 4 srs. and the buffalo had to be taken to low hills before winter.
neutral_summary: Severe climate and high altitude prevent buffalo rearing in Brahmaur, causing sharp drop in milk yield and forcing winter removal to the plains.
term_notes: Seer (sr) is traditional measure (~0.93 kg); low hills refers to Kangra/Punjab borderlands.
coder_notes: Crucial explanation for complete absence of buffaloes in village census despite presence in OCR text.

original_excerpt: It is interesting to note that all the three blacksmiths and 2 silversmiths are Sipis and Reharas respectively. It will also be worthwhile to mention that the above table indicates only the primary occupations of the villagers, and instances are not lacking when a man with agriculture as his primary occupation has sheep and goats rearing as his subsidiary occupation.
neutral_summary: Artisanal metalworking is strictly stratified along caste lines (Sipis for ironwork, Reharas for silverware), while agriculture and pastoralism operate as multi-tiered subsidiary livelihoods.
term_notes: Sipi and Rehara represent artisan castes within the traditional Gaderan hierarchy.
coder_notes: Demonstrates caste-based craft specialization and dual livelihoods.

original_excerpt: The Sipis are the traditional weavers and tailors of the Gaddis. They wash the wool, spin it into yarn and weave the pattu and gardu blankets, and stitch the chola and dora.
neutral_summary: Sipis perform hereditary textile processing, weaving woolen tweed (pattu) and blankets (gardu), and tailoring the distinctive Gaddi costume.
term_notes: Chola is woollen frock; dora is black woollen rope sash; pattu is coarse woolen tweed.
coder_notes: Demonstrates essential economic interdependence in sheep-wool processing and attire.

original_excerpt: At the Shiva Nawala, the priest is usually a Brahman, but the Sipi acts as the traditional musician and drummer (dholak player) and receives the neck portion of the sacrificed sheep and grain.
neutral_summary: Ritual ceremony honoring Lord Shiva where Brahmin performs liturgical rites while Sipi provides sacred drumming and receives customary meat and grain shares.
term_notes: Nawala is central thanksgiving sacrifice to Lord Shiva among all Gaddi strata.
coder_notes: Direct proof of ritual interdependence across high and low caste boundaries.

page_section: p. 11, Society (Brahmin Apex and Land Inducements)
original_excerpt: The Brahmins occupy the apex of the pyramid representing the caste hierarchy... Rajputs, the original founders of Chamba State, felt that without the Brahmin priests it could not be possible for them to perform religious rites. They invited them from the low-lying areas and offered inducements in the form of giving lands. Most of them entered the State during the period of Meru-Varman who constructed a large number of temples.
neutral_summary: Brahmin dominance in Chitrari originated from historical royal land grants by Rajput rulers (Meru-Varman) to maintain temple worship and ritual legitimacy.
term_notes: Refers to historic Sasana/Agrahara land endowments establishing temple-centered settlements.
coder_notes: Explains Brahmin demographic predominance (77% of population) and landownership.

original_excerpt: The dominance of one caste group led to the subordinate castes practically depending upon them... Aryas and Halis live aloof. Halis are the traditional ploughmen who cultivate land for the Brahmins under customary arrangements, but have adopted the Arya Samaj name to improve status.
neutral_summary: Brahmin landed dominance created structural economic dependence among Halis who performed plowing labour and later mobilized through Arya Samaj reform.
term_notes: Hali derived from hal (plough); Arya Samaj provided anti-untouchability identity.
coder_notes: Illustrates traditional agrarian dependence transitioning into socio-religious mobilization.

page_section: p. 45, Economy (Rainy Season Gujjar Milk Trade)
original_excerpt: Milk, therefore, does not form part of their daily diet and is practically non-existent. Even for the purpose of tea, powder milk is to be used. But during the rainy season the Gujjars (a nomadic tribe dealing with milk and its products) come in the nearby areas and settle on the dhars and from there the milk can however, be purchased.
neutral_summary: Severe shortage of local milk in Chitrari forces settled villagers to depend upon visiting nomadic Gujjars who camp on high alpine ridges (dhars) during monsoon.
term_notes: Dhars are alpine grazing pastures; highlights commercial pastoral-agrarian symbiosis.
coder_notes: Primary evidence of seasonal inter-community trade linking sedentary Hindus and pastoral Muslims.

original_excerpt: Bensis—This is the smaller caste and is traditionally engaged in playing music and pipes at temples and festive occasions, receiving customary dues from the villagers.
neutral_summary: Hereditary community of temple musicians performing at religious ceremonies in exchange for traditional village dues.
term_notes: Bensi is customary musical performer caste attached to Shakti Devi temple.
coder_notes: Documents specialized ceremonial service group in temple village economy.

original_excerpt: The houses are scattered over the mohal in 13 hamlets. Except Maingal hamlet which has 7 houses closely built, other hamlets consist of one or two houses only. Maingal inhabited by Brahmins is surrounded by Gujjar hamlets on three sides... Gujjars do not have separate cattle sheds. Their kothas are divided internally.
neutral_summary: Settlement pattern reflects occupational cleavage: nuclear Brahmin cluster at Maingal surrounded by dispersed Gujjar forest hamlets inhabiting combined dwelling-byre kothas.
term_notes: Kotha is flat-roofed rough stone and timber pastoral dwelling.
coder_notes: Captures spatial manifestation of occupational and religious differentiation.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Lohar Ironwork and Khalian Remuneration)
original_excerpt: The Lohar households repair the iron agricultural implements for cultivators. They do not charge cash fees but receive customary shares of unhusked grain (khalian) directly from the threshing floors at each harvest.
neutral_summary: Village blacksmiths maintain agricultural iron tools under customary jajmani barter, compensated in grain shares at harvest rather than cash.
term_notes: Khalian is customary harvest grain perquisites given at the threshing floor (khala).
coder_notes: Crucial evidence proving traditional customary service barter operating alongside cash economy.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Gujjar Buffalo Dairying and Ghee Trade)
original_excerpt: All Gujjar households possess buffaloes. Castewise livestock statistics show that in 25 Gujjar households the number of buffaloes is 217... They sell milk locally and convert surplus into clarified butter (ghee) which is carried down to the Chamba town bazaar for sale.
neutral_summary: Muslim Gujjars specialize in commercial buffalo dairying, marketing surplus milk and clarified butter (ghee) in urban Chamba markets.
term_notes: Ghee represents the primary commodified pastoral output linking remote hamlets to urban markets.
coder_notes: Demonstrates market integration of pastoral household economy.

original_excerpt: Muslim Gujjars are the converts from Hindus. But now they have become devout Muslims and practise Islamic customs. It is due to passage of time that they have slowly imbibed the Islamic way of life, yet live in peace with Hindu neighbours.
neutral_summary: Muslim Gujjars maintain distinct Islamic religious identity while maintaining peaceful, interdependent neighbourly relations with orthodox Hindu Brahmins.
term_notes: Highlights peaceful multi-religious co-existence grounded in mutual economic utility.
coder_notes: Directly addresses the religious relations facet of the core research question.

original_excerpt: The term 'Gadi' is a generic name, and under this appellation are included Brahmins, Khatris, and a few Rajputs and Rathis... Impure castes are not styled Gadis, but are known by the names of Badi, Sipi, Hali, &c. They are a semi-pastoral, semi-agricultural race. The greater portion of their wealth consists of flocks of sheep and goats.
neutral_summary: Colonial definition of Gaddi as an occupational-geographic confederation excluding lower service castes like Badi, Sipi, and Hali.
term_notes: Illustrates British colonial boundary-making separating high-caste pastoralists from service castes.
coder_notes: Crucial baseline for tracking historical evolution of caste boundaries.

original_excerpt: Many Gadis cultivate the winter crops or wheat in Kangra, and returning with their flocks grow the summer or rain crop at 'Barmor,' as the province on the other side of the snow is designated... They hold lands on this side and also in Chamba, and in former days were considered subject to both States.
neutral_summary: Dual agro-pastoral cycle and bi-regional land tenure where Gaddis hold property in Kangra and Brahmaur across the high snowy passes.
term_notes: Trans-Himalayan transhumance and dual sovereign allegiance.
coder_notes: Key evidence of ecological adaptation through migration.

original_excerpt: In no-man's-land one makes friends with Gujars and Gaddis.
neutral_summary: Popular regional proverb reflecting the marginal ecological niches and pastoral mobility shared by Gujjars and Gaddis in frontier tracts.
term_notes: Vernacular proverb recorded in colonial census text.
coder_notes: Illustrates shared pastoral reputation across ethnic/religious lines.

original_excerpt: The Gaddis are divided into four classes: (i) Brahmans, (ii) Khatris and Rajputs who regularly wear the sacred thread, (iii) Thakurs and Rathis who usually do not wear it, and (iv) a menial or dependant class, comprising Kolis, Riharas, Lohars, Badhis, Sipi and Halis, to whom the title of Gaddi is incorrectly applied by outsiders as inhabitants of the Gaderan, though the true Gaddis do not acknowledge them as Gaddis at all.
neutral_summary: Four-tier hierarchical taxonomy of Gaddi society distinguishing thread-wearing upper strata from menial dependent artisan castes.
actor_2: Dependent Castes (Kolis, Riharas, Lohars, Badhis, Sipis, Halis)
term_notes: Gaderan denotes the homeland of Gaddis; Janeu marks ritual status.
coder_notes: Foundational text for analyzing social stratification and occupational dependence.

original_excerpt: Sipi,—The weaver of the Gaddi tribes; found in the Barmaur wizarat of the Chamba State, and virtually the same as the Hali. A low hill-caste who are professional sheep-shearers.
neutral_summary: Identifies Sipi as professional wool-shearers and weavers specific to Brahmaur wizarat, equating their status with Halis.
term_notes: Equates Sipi with Hali; pinpoints Brahmaur wizarat as habitat.
coder_notes: Direct historical definition of occupational role in wool production.

original_excerpt: When all other castes are dead make friends with a Gujar... But he is far inferior in both personal character and repute to the Jat. He is lazy to a degree, and a wretched cultivator... while his fondness for cattle extends to those of other people.
neutral_summary: Colonial ethnographic depiction recording pejorative stereotypes of Gujjars as poor cultivators prone to cattle lifting.
term_notes: Demonstrates British colonial bias against nomadic pastoralism versus settled agriculture.
coder_notes: Essential for deconstructing colonial bias in Rose.

page_section: p. 112, Sub Table X, Chamba Summary
original_excerpt: Chamba State: Occupied houses 30,665; Population 146,870; Persons per house 4.79. Rural population overwhelmingly concentrated in small mountainous hamlets.
neutral_summary: Macro-demographic profile of Chamba State showing dispersed settlement density and rural household structure.
term_notes: Macro-demographic baseline for comparing village-level household sizes.
coder_notes: Connects macro-provincial data with micro-village surveys.
